title: Recorded video interviews
objectives: Answer a recorded question in two minutes after thirty seconds of preparation.

screens.title: Where does the answer start?
screens.prose: A candidate's two-minute recorded answer, one sentence a line, with the time each began. The question was "Tell us about a time you worked in a team."

lines: 0:00  Thank you for this opportunity; I'm really excited to be here.
0:09  So, teamwork is something I think is very important.
0:16  There are lots of times I've worked in teams, at school and at university.
0:25  Let me think about which one to pick.
0:30  Last term I led a team of four on a statistics project with a two-week deadline.
0:39  Two days in, our data had 15% missing values, and we disagreed on what to do.
0:49  I split the work: two of us cleaned the data, two built the model.
0:58  I set a 15-minute check-in each morning so no one was blocked.
1:07  We handed in a day early and scored 78%, the top mark on the module.
1:22  I learned to agree the plan before splitting the work.
1:34  On a trading desk, a team acts on one view at once, so that habit matters.
1:50  I would bring it to the internship from the first week.

explain.text: The answer starts at line 5, at 0:30, after four lines of warm-up. A quarter of the 2 minutes is gone before the story starts. A reviewer marking many answers may stop listening by then.

screens.prose: That was a **recorded video interview**. The format is reported for a bank's recorded round in l4 (October 2026). Check the instructions screen each time; formats vary.

rows: One at a time, shown on screen

screens.question: The four warm-up lines ran from 0:00 to 0:30. What share of the 2-minute answer is that?

hints.text: Thirty seconds out of how many?
Two minutes is 120 seconds.

feedback.correct: A quarter of the answer, gone on warm-up.

byKey.third: You used 100 seconds. Two minutes is 120.
byKey.half: You used one minute. The answer is two minutes long.

explain.text: $30 / 120 = 25\%$ of the time went before the answer started. The format allows one take, so that quarter cannot be won back. Source: candidate reports gathered for l4, October 2026; check each instructions screen.

screens.prose: A better shape: answer the question in the first sentence (10 s). Tell one story (80 s). Close by tying it to the role (30 s).

screens.question: Drag the two boundaries to give the sections those times.

hints.text: Running totals again.
The first sentence ends at 10 s.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each boundary is a running total.

byKey.a1: Boundary 1 ends the first sentence, at 10 s.

explain.text: The first sentence answers at once, so the reviewer knows where you are going. The story takes 80 s and the close 30 s. At 130 words a minute the whole answer is about 260 words.

screens.prose: The shape you dragged is one budget: $$\underbrace{10}_{\text{answer}} + \underbrace{80}_{\text{story}} + \underbrace{30}_{\text{close}} = 120 \text{ s}$$ At a calm 130 words a minute, $t$ seconds hold $130 \times t / 60$ words.
screens.question: About how many words is the 80-second story?

hints.text: What fraction of a minute is 80 s?
$130 \times 4/3 \approx 173$ words.

byKey.all: That is the whole answer. The story is 80 of the 120 seconds.
byKey.per-s: You used one word a second.

explain.text: $130 \times \tfrac{80}{60} \approx 173$ words. As a check, two thirds of 260 is about 173. That is room for one situation, what you did and a result with a number.

screens.prose: You get about 30 seconds before the camera starts. How should you use them?
screens.question: Which plan works best?

options.text: Note three words that carry the story
Write a full script and read it
options.why: You wrote a script. You cannot write 260 words in 30 s, and reading takes your eyes off the camera.
You skipped preparation. Without a plan, the warm-up lines from the hook come back.

options.text: Spend it choosing between five stories
options.why: You spent the time choosing. Keep a short story list ready, as in l11, so you only pick.

hints.text: What can you write in 30 seconds that keeps you on track?
A few words, not sentences.
Three words: the situation, the problem, the result.

feedback.correct: Three words, eyes on the camera.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what fits in 30 seconds.

explain.text: Three words are enough to keep the story in order. A script cannot be written in 30 seconds and pulls your eyes down. Know your stories beforehand, so the 30 seconds are for choosing and noting.

screens.prose: The reviewer sees and hears only what the camera gives them. Here is one candidate's set-up.

rows: Laptop on a pile of books, lens at eye level
On your knees, looking up at you

screens.question: Select all that apply: which choices help the recording?

options.why: You kept the window. Bright light behind you turns your face into a silhouette.
You kept the low laptop. The camera looks up your nose and wobbles as you move.

hints.text: Can the reviewer see your face and hear you clearly?
Light should fall on your face, not behind it.
Eye-level camera, lamp in front, quiet room, plain wall. Not the window or the low laptop.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep what makes your face and voice clear.

explain.text: Eye level, light in front, a quiet room and a plain wall give a clear, steady picture. A window behind you darkens your face. A low laptop gives an unflattering angle and shakes.

explain.text: Settling a disagreement with data is close to persuading with it, so it fits with one honest clause. Reviewers prefer a true near fit to an invented exact one. The instructions screen says whether a retake exists; usually it does not.

ideas: A recorded round: one question, about 30 s to prepare, about 2 minutes to answer, usually one take.
Answer in the first sentence (10 s), tell one story (80 s), close on the role (30 s).

summary.trap: A long warm-up, or one memorised answer forced onto every question.

quiz.question: Select all that apply: which are reported features of a recorded video round?

options.text: A live interviewer who asks follow-ups
options.why: You described a live round. A recorded one is watched later.

feedback.correct: Short preparation, two minutes, one take.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recorded means no one is there live.

explain.text: The question appears, you prepare for about 30 seconds and answer for about 2 minutes, usually once. Someone watches it later.

quiz.question: Which first sentence is best for "Tell us about a time you showed leadership"?

options.text: "Last year I ran my hall's charity quiz, with 12 volunteers."
"Thank you for having me; it's great to be here."
options.why: You opened with thanks. It uses time and answers nothing.

options.text: "Leadership means different things to different people."
options.why: You opened with a definition. The reviewer asked for a time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Answer in the first sentence.

explain.text: The first sentence names the example, so the reviewer knows the answer is coming. Thanks and definitions delay it.

quiz.question: Your only quiet room has a bright window. Where should it be?

options.text: In front of you, behind the camera

options.why: You put it behind. Your face becomes a silhouette.
It matters. Light behind you darkens your face on camera.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Light should fall on your face.

explain.text: Light from in front falls on your face. Light from behind leaves your face dark against a bright window.

quiz.question: At 130 words a minute, about how many words fit in a 2-minute answer?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Two minutes at 130 a minute.

explain.text: $130 \times 2 = 260$ words: about half a page, or one story told well.
